newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil plans second biggest Indian reserve.
newsitem.headline: Brazil plans second biggest Indian reserve.

text.p: Brazil plans to turn a chunk of rainforest the size of Portugal into its second largest Indian reserve, still unsure how many tribes living there have never met a "white man," a leading anthropologist said.

Sydney Possuelo, Brazil's top Indian expert, said he hoped that by year's end the government would have begun demarcating 20.5 million acres (8.3 million hectares) of Amazon jungle in the Javari Valley on the violence-torn border with Peru.

"We hope the demarcation process will have begun this year. With God's help, it will proceed smoothly," the 57-year-old former head of Brazil's National Indian Foundation (Funai) said in one of several interviews this week.

Almost 10 percent of Brazil's landmass has been identified as belonging to the country's 300,000-odd Indians, down from five million when the Portuguese first arrived in 1500. The Javari Valley, once it is demarcated in a process that may take years, will be second in size only to Brazil's Yanomami reservation on its northern Amazonian border with Venezuela.
It is home to five tribes that are in touch with the outside world but at least three other uncontacted tribes are believed to live there.

Last October a team led by Possuelo made the first friendly contact by outsiders with the isolated Korubo tribe, which has been pushed deeper and deeper into the rainforest by loggers. The 200 to 300 Korubo have regarded all newcomers as enemies, meeting them with poison darts and clubs, and have killed nine Funai officials in recent expeditions.

"The Korubo has always woken up and looked around, thinking everything out there is his enemy. It was dangerous work contacting them," said Possuelo, who currently heads Funai's Isolated Indians Division.
But Indians were not the only danger in the Javari Valley. Possuelo has contracted malaria 34 times during a long career.

The reserve was originally identified 12 years ago and last year the federal government issued a decree prohibiting non-Indians from entering. Funai's efforts to create the reserve have angered drug smugglers in neighbouring Colombia and Peru as well as Brazilians who want to exploit the timber.

Mayors of the towns of Atalaia do Norte, Tabatinga and Tonantins, along with the Bishop of the Alto Solimoes Diocese, Don Alcimar Magalhaes, have ganged up against Possuelo and accused him of being "arbitrary, authoritarian and violent" in his drive to stop locals from entering Indian land.

"I have nothing against Indians but I am against the behaviour of this man who is treating our people with disrespect," said federal Deputy Euler Ribeiro, who on behalf of the mayors has asked the government to fire Possuelo.

Ribeiro acknowledges that the bishop is related to one of the region's largest timber merchants and agrees that local concerns about the Indian reserve centre on economics. But he feels the white people of the Javari are suffering "disproportionate" treatment and he demands "social justice".

"There's only a few dozen Indians there. That's an awful lot of land for them to walk around in, and remember these Indians are mainly ill or anaemic. They don't walk much," the deputy, a retired doctor, told Reuters.
"This is the sort of thing, political pressure, that could still hurt the process of demarcation," Possuelo said.
